claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed by formation of a stable surface oxide layer.
The surface oxide layer is stable at high temperature.
The oxide layer inhibits chemical reactions that would degrade the nanoalloy.
The initial high-entropy nanoalloy has a random elemental distribution.
An oxide-coated high-entropy nanoalloy will have improved high-temperature stability relative to an uncoated nanoalloy.
An oxide-coated high-entropy nanoalloy will resist degradation better than an uncoated nanoalloy.
The prediction applies from 500 to 1000 °C in an inert atmosphere.
The prediction is bounded to oxide layers thinner than 10 nm.
Oxide-layer composition and microstructure may influence stability.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes stability to oxide-layer formation during high-temperature exposure, but the specified atmosphere is inert and no oxygen source or pre-existing oxide is identified.

The stated intervention is only high-temperature exposure and the hypothesis concerns oxide formation, whereas the proposed comparison uses predesignated coated and uncoated samples. This tests the effect of an added coating rather than whether heating causes the proposed oxide mediator to form.
